text: Your weak places aren't where God gives up on you. They're where His power gets to flow.
explanation:
Paul pleaded three times for relief from a messenger of Satan sent to harass his ministry. The Lord answered, "My grace is sufficient for you, for My strength is made perfect in weakness." The word for strength is dunamis, the root of our word dynamite. So Paul concluded, "Most gladly I will rather boast in my infirmities… for when I am weak, then I am strong."

We curate our strengths and hide our weaknesses. But a lifeguard can't save a drowning man while he's still thrashing in his own strength; he'll pull the rescuer under. Don't rejoice in the weakness itself; rejoice that it makes room for God's power. Wherever strength has broken down in your life, that's the very place He promises to rebuild.

text: In Genesis 1:1, the middle word of seven is untranslated: aleph-tav, the first and last letters. "I am the Alpha and the Omega."
explanation:
In Hebrew, the Bible's first verse has exactly seven words and twenty-eight letters, multiples of seven, the number of perfection. At its centre stands a little word left untranslated in English: et, spelled aleph-tav, the first and last letters of the Hebrew alphabet. In Greek, that's Alpha and Omega, the title Jesus gives Himself in Revelation.

It's like a signature at the heart of creation. "All things were made through Him, and without Him nothing was made." And whatever variants or troubles fill the alphabet in between, He's both the first and the last. He has the final word.

text: "The Lord blessed [aleph-tav] Obed-Edom." When David "brought up [aleph-tav] the ark," he did it with gladness.
explanation:
The same untranslated aleph-tav appears in the Hebrew of the verses about Obed-Edom's blessing and David bringing up the ark to Zion. Before Uzzah's death, David's words were full of I, me, my. "How can the ark of the Lord come to me?" But when he set out to lift up the ark, the picture of Christ, and put it at the centre, there was gladness.

"In Him all things consist": they're held together. Physicists still can't fully explain what holds the atom together. Take the hub out of a wheel and the spokes fall apart. Put Jesus at the centre of your marriage, work, health and parenting, and He holds it together.

text: "From the time that he made Joseph overseer of his house… the Lord blessed the Egyptian's house for Joseph's sake."
explanation:
Potiphar was an Egyptian with no covenant. But notice the timing: the blessing began "from the time" he put Joseph in charge, and "the blessing of the Lord was on all that he had in the house and in the field."

Joseph is one of the clearest pictures of Christ in the Old Testament: loved by his father, rejected by his brothers, and the bread of life to the world. Make Jesus the overseer of everything you have. The blessing doesn't depend on how impressive you are. It comes "for Joseph's sake," for Jesus' sake.

text: Don't try to love that difficult colleague. Say, "Lord, You've got this," and watch His love flow.
explanation:
"I'll make an effort to say something nice tomorrow." That's human strength, and it tends to produce the opposite. If anger is your weakness, watch the first reaction. When someone pushes your button, rest inside: "Lord, You've got this."

You'll often get to the end of the day and realise you never lost your cool, and you've been kind without trying. That's the Christian life: Christ living in you. "Let us labour to enter that rest": the work is to stop trying. Rest isn't doing nothing. It's activity led by the Spirit, like power steering, where you choose the direction and the power does the turning.

text: Talk about Him with your children as you sit, walk, lie down and rise up, "that your days… may be like the days of heaven on earth."
explanation:
God told Israel to lay His words in their hearts and teach them to their children, not only in formal lessons but in the flow of everyday life: at home, on the road, at bedtime, in the morning. The result: "that your days and the days of your children may be multiplied… like the days of the heavens above the earth." Long life, and good life.

In the Hebrew, the aleph-tav sign is there again. For you, these are words about Jesus. Share what He's showing you, a sentence here and there, even when your kids seem more interested in their games. The Holy Spirit makes those words stick.

text: Like the bush Moses saw: burning, yet not consumed. Burn up for God, but don't burn out.
explanation:
Living by grace isn't passive or lazy. Jesus was the most restful man who ever lived, and yet He finished everything the Father gave Him in three and a half years. When the energy isn't your own, you can keep burning without being used up.

"The love of Christ compels us." Picture swimming upstream when a surge of floodwater comes; however strong you are, you're carried along. Be conscious of His love for you, and that love will carry you into loving your spouse, your children and the people around you, with fire that doesn't burn out.
